title.en: The past tense: one rule, four endings

card: Drop **-ть** from the infinitive and add **-л** (masc.), **-ла** (fem.), **-ло** (neut.), **-ли** (plural): **чита́ть → чита́л, чита́ла, чита́ло, чита́ли**. The past agrees in **gender**, not person: **я чита́л** (a man), **я чита́ла** (a woman).

sections.body: The Russian past tense was once a participle, something like *I [am] having-read*. That's why it agrees in gender and number like an adjective, and why it doesn't change for person: **я / ты / он чита́л** are all the same. Only the subject's gender and number matter.

sections.title: Stress and irregular pasts
sections.body:
Many short verbs shift the stress to the ending in the feminine only: **жил, жила́, жи́ло, жи́ли**; **был, была́, бы́ло, бы́ли**; **дал, дала́**. Verbs ending in **-ти**, **-чь** or **-зть** have irregular masculine forms:

- **идти́ → шёл, шла, шло, шли**
- **мочь → мог, могла́, могли́**
- **есть → ел, е́ла, е́ли**
- **нести́ → нёс, несла́**
- verbs in **-нуть** often drop the **-ну-**: **исче́знуть → исче́з, исче́зла**

sections.title: Agreement
sections.body:
- With **я** and **ты**, the ending shows the speaker's gender: a woman writes **я была́ ра́да**.
- **вы** always takes **-ли**, even for one person: **Вы бы́ли пра́вы.**
- Neuter and impersonal sentences use **-ло**: **Бы́ло хо́лодно.** **Мне нра́вилось.**
- **у меня́ был / была́ / бы́ло / бы́ли** agrees with the thing possessed: **У меня́ была́ соба́ка.**

English *I read, I was reading, I have read, I had read* all use the same Russian tense; the difference between *was reading* and *have read* is carried by **aspect** (see the next articles): **я чита́л** (imperfective: was reading, used to read) vs **я прочита́л** (perfective: read it through, finished).

mistakes.why: The past agrees with the subject's gender.
**идти́** has an irregular past: **шёл, шла, шли**.

examples.en: Yesterday I was reading a book.
